blocks.text: Merging adapters is the process of permanently combining a trained LoRA low rank update back into the original frozen base weight matrix, producing a single, ordinary weight matrix indistinguishable in structure from a fully fine-tuned model.

This ability to merge cleanly back into the base model is a specific advantage LoRA has over some other PEFT methods, and understanding when and how to merge, versus when to keep the adapter separate, matters directly for deployment decisions.
1. What Merging Actually Means

blocks.alt: A frozen base weight plus a low rank update combine into one merged weight

blocks.text: Merging takes the frozen original weight matrix and the trained low rank update, scaled by alpha as covered in the previous topic, and adds them together permanently, producing one ordinary weight matrix that already contains the fine-tuning adjustment baked directly in.
2. Why LoRA Can Merge While Adapters Typically Cannot

blocks.alt: A traditional adapter is a separate extra layer while LoRA adds directly into the existing weight

blocks.text: The adapter tuning method covered earlier in this module inserts entirely new layers into the network computation path, which cannot simply be folded back into an existing weight matrix. LoRA, by contrast, produces an update that lives in exactly the same shape as the original weight it modifies, making a clean, direct merge possible.
3. The Merge Operation, Mathematically

blocks.alt: The original weight goes through the merge operation to produce a single updated matrix

blocks.text: The merge operation is straightforward, add the scaled low rank update, computed exactly as covered in the Alpha topic, directly to the original frozen weight, producing one combined matrix that behaves identically to the unmerged version but no longer requires the separate LoRA matrices to be applied at runtime.

code.content:
# The merge operation
scaling_factor = alpha / rank
merged_weight = original_weight + scaling_factor * (matrix_a @ matrix_b)
# merged_weight can now replace original_weight entirely

blocks.text: 4. Merged vs Unmerged Deployment

blocks.alt: A merged model has no extra latency while an unmerged model stays swappable

blocks.text: A merged model runs with zero additional inference latency compared to the original base model, since there is no separate adapter computation happening at runtime, everything is already baked into one ordinary weight matrix. An unmerged model keeps the adapter separate, adding a small amount of runtime overhead but preserving the ability to swap adapters without touching the base weights.

blocks.text: 5. Merging Multiple LoRA Adapters Together

blocks.alt: Adapter A and adapter B can merge sequentially

blocks.text: Multiple trained LoRA adapters can, in some cases, be merged sequentially or combined with weighting into one final model, similar in spirit to the adapter fusion idea covered earlier in this module, though the specific approach and quality depend heavily on how related the adapters underlying tasks actually are.
6. When Merging Is the Right Choice

blocks.alt: A final, single purpose deployment favors merging, otherwise keep the adapter unmerged

blocks.text: Merging makes sense once a fine-tuning project has settled on one final, stable configuration meant for a single, dedicated deployment purpose, since the resulting model is simpler to deploy and carries no runtime overhead, at the cost of losing the flexibility to swap the adjustment out later.
7. When to Keep Adapters Unmerged

Keeping adapters unmerged makes more sense during active experimentation, when comparing several candidate adapters against each other, or in a multi-tenant deployment scenario where different customers or tasks need different adapters swapped in against one shared base model, echoing the storage efficiency benefits covered in the earlier Why PEFT topic.
8. Merging and Model Distribution

A merged model can be distributed and used exactly like any other fully fine-tuned model, with no special LoRA aware tooling required to load and run it, which can simplify deployment in environments where the extra infrastructure to apply an adapter at runtime is not readily available.
9. Risks of Merging Incorrectly

blocks.alt: Applying the wrong scaling factor during merging produces a broken merge

blocks.text: Merging requires applying the exact same scaling factor, derived from alpha and rank, that was used during training, applying a different or incorrect scaling during the merge produces a model that behaves differently from the trained, evaluated adapter, a subtle bug worth checking carefully before finalizing a merge.
Worked Example

A team finishes experimenting with several candidate LoRA adapters trained for slightly different variations of a support tone task, keeping them all unmerged and swappable while comparing evaluation results across the candidates.

Once they settle on the best performing adapter, they merge it permanently into the base model for their production deployment, since they only need this one final configuration going forward, gaining the zero overhead inference speed of a merged model without needing to maintain the ability to swap adapters they no longer plan to use.
Common Mistakes

items: Merging with the wrong scaling factor, producing a model that no longer matches its evaluated performance
Merging too early, during active experimentation, losing the flexibility to easily compare different adapter candidates
Assuming every PEFT method supports clean merging the way LoRA does, when methods like adapter tuning typically do not
Forgetting that a merged model can no longer be easily separated back into base weights plus adapter

blocks.text: Practice

For a LoRA setup with a chosen rank and alpha, write out the exact merge formula you would apply, confirming you understand precisely what scaling factor needs to be included for the merge to correctly match the trained adapter behavior.
Key Takeaway

Merging permanently folds a trained LoRA low rank update back into the original base weight, producing a model with zero inference overhead at the cost of losing adapter swap flexibility, a capability unique to LoRA among the PEFT methods covered in this module, and the right choice specifically once a fine-tuning project has settled on its final, stable configuration.
